title: The Friend Who Became Successful First
description: When his engineering roommate raises twenty-eight million dollars and buys a penthouse overlooking the Indiranagar canopy, freelance designer Siddharth Rao confronts the quiet, poisonous agony of peer comparison—and the courage it takes to love a friend whose ascent leaves you behind.
excerpt: The first thing that changes when your best friend becomes rich is not his affection; it is his velocity.
author: Noble John Steeven
coverImageAlt: Two plastic terrace chairs on a Bangalore rooftop at night, overlooking the distant glittering towers of an IT corridor under a purple evening sky

storySections.chapterTitle: I. Movement One: The Terrace of Equals (2016)
storySections.heading: I. Movement One: The Terrace of Equals (2016)
storySections.body:
The first thing that changes when your best friend becomes rich is not his affection; it is his velocity.

In the autumn of 2016, Gautam Nair and I lived on the roof of a three-story residential building in Koramangala 5th Block, squeezed into an unauthorized asbestos-roofed studio that the landlord, a retired sub-registrar named Muniswamappa, rented to us for nine thousand rupees a month.

The studio had two pieces of furniture: a queen-sized coir mattress that we slept on head-to-toe to avoid breathing each other's stale beer fumes, and two white plastic Nilkamal armchairs that sat outside on the terrace gravel beside an abandoned concrete water tank.

Those two chairs were our parliament.

Every evening after seven, when the heat radiated off the black tar roof into the cool Bangalore breeze, we would sit there with our laptops balanced on our knees. Gautam was twenty-four, gaunt, with a perpetually untrimmed stubble and a habit of chewing the inside of his lower lip until it bled. He had quit his forty-thousand-rupee software engineering job at Infosys six months earlier to build an open-source API gateway for local cooperative banks.

I was a freelance UI designer, charging six hundred rupees an hour to design WordPress landing pages for fitness trainers in Indiranagar and dental clinics in Jayanagar.

We had no money. We had so little money that on Tuesday nights, when our shared SBI account dipped below the five-hundred-rupee minimum balance penalty threshold, we would pool our change on the kitchen counter: twenty-eight rupees in coins, an empty packet of classic milds, and two vouchers for free cold coffee at a café on 80 Feet Road that had expired three months ago.

We would walk down to the street cart behind Jyoti Nivas College, buy two plates of egg Maggi cooked with extra green chilies and chopped onions for thirty rupees each, and eat them sitting on the terrace parapet.

Our whiteboard was the rear surface of Muniswamappa's water tank. Gautam had stolen a blue whiteboard marker from his old cubicle at Infosys, but because the concrete was unpainted and porous, the ink had soaked permanently into the stone. The formulas for retry logic, idempotency keys, and socket timeouts were preserved there like prehistoric cave paintings.

'When PaySprint hits ten thousand daily transactions,' Gautam told me one night in November, pointing his plastic fork toward the red neon glow of the Forum Mall in the distance, 'I'm going to buy a twelve-hundred-cc Triumph Bonneville. Black paint. Spoke wheels. I'll park it right in front of Muniswamappa's gate and leave the engine idling for fifteen minutes every morning just to listen to the exhaust.'

'Muniswamappa will call the police,' I said.

'Muniswamappa will ask for a ride,' Gautam said, grinning his lopsided, hungry grin.

In those years, our poverty was not a hardship; it was an aesthetic. It was the common currency of our youth. Because neither of us had anything, everything we shared—a jar of peanut butter, an ACT Fibernet broadband password, a three-pin power strip that sparked if you touched the ground pin—was an emblem of an absolute, unquestioned brotherhood.

We were equals because our failures were identical in scale. What neither of us understood, sitting on those white plastic chairs under the Bangalore stars, was that equality between young men is often nothing more than a temporary truce enforced by mutual bankruptcy.

storySections.chapterTitle: II. Movement Two: The Series A Tab (2019)
storySections.heading: II. Movement Two: The Series A Tab (2019)
storySections.body:
The rift did not open with an argument. It opened with an article on the fourth page of the Economic Times on a Tuesday in August 2019.

The headline was three columns wide: *Bangalore Fintech PaySprint Raises $4.2M Series A Led by Sequoia India*.

There was a photograph of Gautam standing in front of a white brick wall in their new office on 100 Feet Road. He was wearing a fitted navy polo shirt, crisp grey chinos, and clean white leather sneakers. His hair was cut by a stylist; the frantic, feral hunger that had characterized his twenties had been replaced by the quiet, radiant posture of a young man who had been told by three venture capitalists that his instincts were worth thirty-two million dollars.

He called me at four that afternoon.

'Siddharth. Pack your laptop. Toit at eight. Don't be late.'

When I arrived at the brewpub on 100 Feet Road, the place was packed with the usual Friday evening crowd of software engineers, venture associates, and agency account directors. Gautam had reserved the long wooden table on the mezzanine. Around him were eight of his earliest engineers—boys who had joined when the company was still operating out of our terrace bedroom—along with two product managers from Flipkart he had hired the previous month.

Gautam saw me on the stairs. He stood up, knocked his wooden stool back, and threw both arms around my neck, squeezing me so hard my glasses slipped.

'Look at this guy!' he shouted to the table, his face flushed with triumph. 'This is the man who drew our first logo! On a cracked iPad in 2016 while eating cold biryani!'

The engineers laughed and raised their beer mugs. I smiled. I felt a surge of genuine, incandescent pride for him. I had watched him vomit into Muniswamappa's drainage pipe from sheer exhaustion during the three weeks when the ICICI integration servers kept rejecting his webhook payloads. He had earned every dollar of that valuation.

Then the evening progressed, and the subtle mechanics of wealth began to assert themselves.

Gautam ordered without looking at the right-hand column of the menu. He ordered three pitchers of Tint-in-Wit, two platters of wood-fired beef pizzas, four bowls of spicy chicken wings, and three rounds of single malt whiskey for the senior leads.

Every forty-five minutes, his phone would vibrate against the wooden tabletop. He would turn the screen toward his palm, squint at the notification, and swipe it away. Once, the screen remained lit for three seconds: it was a message from a partner at a sovereign wealth fund in Singapore asking if he was free for a breakfast call at the Leela Palace on Thursday.

At midnight, when the bar announced last call, the waiter brought the leather folder holding the bill.

Out of muscle memory—the unthinking, seven-year habit of two middle-class boys who always split the auto-rickshaw fare down to the nearest ten-rupee coin—I reached into my back pocket and pulled out my worn leather wallet.

'Gautam,' I said, pulling out two five-hundred-rupee notes. 'What's my share?'

Gautam didn't even look at my money.

He reached into his front pocket, pulled out a matte-black metal credit card, and tossed it onto the folder with the casual, negligent flick of a wrist you use to discard a bus ticket.

'Don't be an idiot, Sid,' he said, his voice completely casual, completely devoid of malice. 'Put that away.'

The bill was eighteen thousand six hundred rupees.

Eighteen thousand six hundred rupees was three-quarters of my monthly rent for the 1BHK I had moved into in Ejipura. It was four days of freelance illustration work. For Gautam, it was a rounding error on an expense account that would be reimbursed by morning.

He didn't mean to insult me. That was the terrible, unforgivable part of it. If he had been arrogant, if he had smirked or made a show of his generosity, I could have hated him. I could have turned his wealth into a moral defect and comforted myself with my own virtue.

Instead, his generosity was clean, effortless, and unthinking. And in that effortless gesture, he had quietly dismantled the foundation of our brotherhood. He had made me a dependent at his feast.

I put the two crumpled five-hundred-rupee notes back into my pocket. My face burned with a heat that had nothing to do with the craft beer. I sat there in the loud, echoing brewpub, surrounded by people cheering his name, and realized that my oldest friend had stepped into an orbit where I could only ever be an observer.

storySections.heading: III. The Divergent Vocabulary (2020–2021)
storySections.body:
Between 2020 and 2021, our conversations died a slow, linguistic death.

When two people live in different economic strata, it is not their feelings that diverge first; it is their nouns.

My nouns were local, tactile, and precarious. I spoke of client payment delays, the TDS deductions that took seven months to recover from the income tax portal, the landlord who refused to fix the seepage behind my bathroom mirror, and the price of tender coconut on the Ejipura main road going from thirty-five to fifty rupees.

Gautam's nouns were abstract, global, and frictionless.

When we met for breakfast at Airlines Hotel on Sunday mornings—the only time his calendar showed an open ninety-minute slot—he spoke of 'burn multiples,' 'secondary share sales,' 'regulatory tailwinds in Southeast Asia,' and 'talent retention tranches.'

He would arrive in an electric sedan with tinted glass, wearing an Apple Watch that buzzed every three minutes to remind him to stand up or take a deep breath.

'You should stop doing freelance scraps, Sid,' he told me once over a plate of khara bath. 'Come in-house at PaySprint. I'll create a VP of Brand Design role for you. Thirty lakhs base, plus half a percent in ESOPs. In three years, that half-percent will be worth two crores.'

He thought he was offering me a lifeline.

He did not understand that to accept a salary from him—to have my performance reviewed by my oldest friend, to have my rent paid by his enterprise—would be the final surrender of my dignity.

'I like working for myself, Gautam,' I said, scraping the ghee off the steel spoon. 'I like setting my own hours.'

He looked at me with that specific, pitying indulgence that successful tech entrepreneurs reserve for people who believe in artistic autonomy.

'Sure,' he said softly. 'Whatever you say, boss.'

He called me 'boss' when he didn't want to argue. It was the verbal equivalent of patting a child on the head before leaving the room.

The envy came in the dark, usually after midnight.

I would sit in my dark living room in Ejipura, the light of my monitor reflecting off the bare wall, scrolling through LinkedIn or Twitter. I would see his name quoted in Forbes: *Gautam Nair on the Future of Cross-Border Liquidity*. I would read comments from twenty-two-year-old IIT graduates calling him a visionary, a genius, an inspiration.

A cold, greasy sickness would spread through my gut.

I wanted him to succeed—truly, I did. If someone had threatened his company, I would have defended him with my fists. But at the same time, in the rotten, unexamined cellar of my soul, a small, vicious voice whispered: *What if the Reserve Bank changes the payment aggregator rules? What if the next round falls through? What if he comes back to earth, just for six months, so we can sit on the plastic chairs again?*

Envy is not the desire to have what another person has. Envy is the unbearable suspicion that the other person's success reveals the absolute mediocrity of your own existence.

storySections.chapterTitle: III-B. The Midnight Ambulance to Aluva (2021)
storySections.heading: III-B. The Midnight Ambulance to Aluva (2021)
storySections.body:
The test of our estrangement came not in a boardroom, but in the sterile, green-tiled corridor of a private hospital in Aluva on a rainy Tuesday in October 2021.

At 3:15 AM, my phone rang. I rarely received calls at that hour; my mother in Hubli slept soundly, and clients only emailed when their staging servers crashed.

It was Gautam's mother, Padmini Aunty.

Her voice was trembling so violently she could barely speak Hindi. Gautam's father, a retired railway station superintendent who had spent thirty years dispatching trains in Shoranur, had suffered an acute myocardial infarction while watching the late news. He had collapsed on the veranda tiles.

'Siddharth mon,' she wept into the receiver, reverting to the Malayalam endearment she had used when we were college students. 'Gautam's phone is switched off. There is an automated voice saying he is in flight. The local clinic doctor says we must transfer him to Aster Medcity immediately, but they are asking for a sixty-thousand-rupee deposit before they dispatch the cardiac ambulance.'

Gautam was at thirty-five thousand feet between Frankfurt and Dubai, returning from a fintech summit in Lisbon.

I looked at my bank account on my phone screen. My freelance balance stood at seventy-four thousand two hundred rupees—the proceeds of an exhausting eight-week brand design contract for a logistics app in Chennai that had taken three months to pay out.

I did not hesitate.

I initiated an IMPS transfer of sixty-five thousand rupees directly to the hospital's billing portal. I called the casualty administrator in Ernakulam, verified the transaction reference number, and stayed on the line until I heard the ambulance sirens pulling into their driveway in Aluva.

Then I caught the 6:00 AM flight from Kempegowda to Cochin.

When Gautam finally landed in Kochi at three in the afternoon, escorted through VIP immigration by two airline representatives, he ran into the third-floor intensive care waiting room with his suitcase wheels spinning wildly.

His father was out of surgery, resting under heavy sedation with two drug-eluting stents in his coronary artery.

Padmini Aunty was sitting on a plastic hospital chair, holding my hand, drinking cold sweet tea from a paper cup I had brought from the hospital canteen.

Gautam stopped in the doorway.

He was wearing his bespoke dark suit, crumpled from twenty hours in business-class cabins, holding a leather briefcase embossed with his initials. He looked at his mother. Then he looked at me—sitting there in my faded denim jacket, with dark rings under my eyes and sixty-five thousand rupees missing from my bank account.

He did not pull out his black metal card.

He walked across the green linoleum floor, dropped his briefcase onto the tiles, and sank down onto his knees in front of my chair. He buried his face in my lap and cried with the desperate, racking sobs of a twelve-year-old boy who has looked over the edge of the world and realized that none of his accomplishments can stop a father's heart from failing.

I put my arm around his shoulders.

'He's okay, Gautam,' I whispered. 'The doctor said the tissue damage is minimal. He's going to be fine.'

For that one afternoon, the twenty-eight million dollars ceased to exist. There were no cap tables, no liquidation preferences, no valuation multiples. There were only two boys from RV College who remembered the taste of cold canteen tea and knew that when life breaks open, the only currency that matters is who shows up at the door.

storySections.chapterTitle: IV. Movement Three: The Penthouse Fire Stairs (2024)
storySections.heading: IV. Movement Three: The Penthouse Fire Stairs (2024)
storySections.body:
In February 2024, Gautam bought a four-thousand-square-foot duplex penthouse on the fourteenth floor of a luxury development on 12th Main, Indiranagar.

The housewarming party was an industry convention.

Two hundred people moved across the Italian travertine marble floors. There were founders of unicorns, two junior partners from venture funds in Menlo Park, a celebrity chef from Mumbai who had set up a live ceviche counter on the balcony, and an acoustic jazz trio playing beside the heated plunge pool.

The view was magnificent. From the terrace, Bangalore stretched out into the night like an illuminated circuit board, the canopy of rain trees in Defence Colony looking like dark, undulating moss beneath the streetlights.

I stood near the bar for an hour, holding a gin-and-tonic I didn't want, wearing my best charcoal blazer that suddenly felt stiff and synthetic beside the bespoke linen shirts of the tech elite.

Nobody spoke to me. When someone asked what I did, I said, 'I'm a brand designer,' and their eyes immediately scanned the room behind my shoulder to see if someone with a larger valuation had entered the foyer.

At 11:30, as the music shifted to ambient electronic, a hand grabbed my elbow.

It was Gautam.

He looked exhausted. His eyes were bloodshot; the collar of his white linen shirt was unbuttoned to the sternum. He smelled of whiskey, expensive cologne, and the sharp, sour sweat of a man who had spent four hours performing charm for people he didn't trust.

'Come here,' he whispered.

He pulled me through a service door beside the pantry, into the cold, concrete stairwell of the emergency fire escape. The heavy fire door clicked shut behind us, cutting off the jazz music, the laughter, and the clinking of champagne flutes with absolute finality.

Gautam sat down on the third concrete step, his back against the raw grey wall.

From inside his jacket, he pulled out a pint bottle of Old Monk rum and two crushed paper cups from the catering station.

'Sit down, Sid,' he said.

I sat beside him on the cold concrete.

He poured two inches of dark rum into each paper cup, passed one to me, and held his cup up against the bare fluorescent tube overhead.

'To Koramangala,' he said.

'To Koramangala,' I echoed.

We drank. The rum burned down my throat—cheap, sweet, vanilla-heavy, exactly the same taste as the eighty-rupee quarters we used to buy from the liquor store beside Jyoti Nivas College in 2016.

For five minutes, neither of us said anything. Through the heavy fire door, we could hear the muffled, rhythmic thud of the party.

'I hate them,' Gautam said quietly, staring down at his scuffed leather loafers.

'Who?'

'All of them. Every single person in that living room.' He rubbed his face with both hands, pressing the heels of his palms into his eye sockets until his knuckles turned white. 'If PaySprint misses our gross margin target next quarter, half of those VCs will start circulating an emergency board resolution to replace me with an ex-Google VP from Singapore. They don't give a damn about me, Sid. They care about their four-times liquidation preference.'

He looked at me. His eyes were wide, naked, and terrified.

'Do you know what I miss?' he asked, his voice trembling slightly. 'I miss sitting on those two broken Nilkamal chairs with you, eating sixty-rupee egg Maggi, and having nobody care whether I lived or died.'

I looked at him.

I looked at the twenty-eight-million-dollar CEO sitting on a dirty concrete fire escape with a crushed paper cup of rum in his hand.

And in that moment, the envy that had poisoned my blood for five years simply dissolved.

It did not dissolve because I felt superior to him, or because I took pleasure in his misery. It dissolved because I finally saw the ledger for what it was.

Gautam had not escaped the trap; he had merely upgraded the cage. He had traded the anxiety of poverty for the terror of obsolescence. He was running on a treadmill that had no off-switch, surrounded by people whose affection was contingent on a quarterly recurring revenue multiple.

And I—with my modest flat in Ejipura, my freelance clients who paid late, and my quiet mornings walking under the rain trees—had something that his twenty-eight million dollars could never purchase: I had the freedom to be ordinary without being destroyed by it.

storySections.heading: V. The True Ledger
storySections.body:
We sat on the fire stairs until the bottle of Old Monk was empty.

We didn't talk about venture rounds, and we didn't talk about my freelance invoices. We talked about Muniswamappa, and the stray dog with three legs that used to sleep outside the bakery on 5th Cross, and the girl from Mount Carmel College Gautam had tried to impress in 2015 by pretending he understood French cinema.

We laughed until our ribs ached. It was the first time in six years that we had laughed without calculating the distance between us.

At 1:30 AM, I stood up. I helped Gautam to his feet, brushed the concrete dust off the seat of his linen trousers, and straightened his collar.

'Go back inside, Nair,' I said. 'Your investors are probably stealing your ceviche.'

He smiled—the old, crooked, hungry smile from the Koramangala roof.

'Call me next Sunday?' he asked.

'Only if you let me buy the dosa,' I said.

He hesitated for a second. Then he nodded. 'Deal. Airlines hotel. Seven-thirty.'

I walked down the fourteen flights of concrete stairs instead of taking the private elevator. My legs were tired, my knees complained at every landing, but with every floor I descended, the air felt cooler, cleaner, and more real.

I stepped out of the building into the cool Bangalore night. The rain trees on 12th Main were dropping pale yellow flowers onto the pavement; the smell of wet asphalt and flowering jasmine hung thick in the air.

I didn't order an Uber. I walked the four kilometers back to Ejipura through the quiet, empty streets.

When I reached my flat, I climbed up to the small terrace on the fourth floor.

I have two white plastic chairs up there too. They cost four hundred rupees each from a plastic store near the bus stand. They are slightly weathered by the monsoon rain, and one of the armrests has a hairline crack near the joint.

I sat down on one of them.

I looked out over the roofs of Ejipura—the water tanks, the dish antennas, the clotheslines swaying in the night wind, the distant towers of the IT corridor twinkling like cold diamonds on the horizon.

I did not want his penthouse. I did not want his cap table, his board meetings, or his sovereign wealth funds.

I loved my friend. I wanted him to survive his fortune. But as I leaned back into the cheap plastic seat and felt the cool night wind against my face, I knew, with the calm and unshakeable certainty of a man who has looked into the fire and stepped back, that my life was my own, and it was enough.
